title_en: How US restrictions on China are reshaping the science race
content_en:
Growing curbs on academic ties have cooled US-China research collaboration and fuelled fears of a brain drain as Beijing surges.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
As the United States and China compete for scientific leadership, Washington and a growing number of states are imposing restrictions on academic ties with China.
Since 2018, Congress and 23 states have introduced 158 bills curbing how US universities work with foreign scientists, students and institutions; 24 became law, according to a new tracker from the Committee of 100, a non-profit organisation of prominent Chinese Americans.
Its interactive map shows 13 states with a law or executive action in place, and states now drive most new bills.
Many of these policies explicitly target China or rely on federal lists that include it, falling most directly on Chinese citizens and others with ties to the country. Chinese-American scholars can also face additional scrutiny, regardless of their citizenship.
Supporters say the rules protect US research from theft by foreign governments. But a growing body of research suggests they are costing American science: collaboration with Chinese researchers has cooled, and many foreign-born scientists say they have considered leaving, while China’s research output keeps climbing.
The interactive map shows current policies in place, with states shaded by how many types of restrictions they have adopted. Restriction types include: Visa and entry, research screening, partnerships and funding, talent recruitment programmes, travel, reporting and disclosure.
“There is so much more administrative oversight about any type of US-China scholarly interaction,” said Gordon Chang, a professor of history at Stanford University.
Chang said the political climate had had a chilling effect, with few willing to speak up. “Everyone’s keeping their head down now,” he said.
Other research warns that falling international student enrolment could cause major economic losses.
Meanwhile, the restrictions have done little to slow Beijing’s scientific rise, according to a report by China’s Ministry of Science and Technology. Over the same period, China has overtaken the US in research and development spending, claimed the top spot in high-impact publications and deepened its research ties with the rest of the world.
The tracker also notes that the national security benefits of the restrictions remain less well measured than their costs.
US restrictions: from the states to Washington
US restrictions span a wide range across the states. Alabama, Arizona, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa and Nebraska mainly require disclosure, meaning universities must report foreign gifts, funding or ties without being barred from them. Arizona, for example, requires public universities to post research security policies and report foreign gifts above US$250,000.
Others go further.
Ohio bars public institutions from accepting gifts from the Chinese government, the Communist Party or the People’s Liberation Army. Louisiana has five of the tracker’s six restriction types, more than any other state: researcher screening, partnership and funding limits, talent recruitment programmes, travel rules and reporting and disclosure requirements.
Students work in a laboratory at Princeton University as part of its international summer research programme. Photo: Handout
The legislative push has cooled from its 2025 peak but has not stopped. The federal government is the only jurisdiction on the tracker with visa and entry restrictions in place.
In 2026, the Pentagon ordered 30 universities to audit and cut risky foreign ties, using a blacklist of 130 mostly Chinese institutions. The audits prompted more than 80 termination-related actions, including Virginia Tech’s early closure of a joint programme with Xidian University.
A looming brain drain in US
Frank Wu, retired president of Queens College of the City University of New York, said US-China academic cooperation had gone through three phases over the past two decades.
It started with initial enthusiasm, followed by suspicion and criminal investigations under the China Initiative, which damaged careers and lives, and now a period of uncertainty, with anti-China sentiment persisting despite growing recognition of the initiative’s excesses.
Publication data suggest that the bilateral research partnership is fading. National Science Foundation data show 23 per cent of internationally co-authored US papers had a Chinese co-author in 2023, down from 27 per cent in 2019.
Researchers also found that US scientists who had collaborated with Chinese scientists became less productive after the National Institutes of Health began investigating foreign influence in research in 2018, compared with peers who collaborated elsewhere.
More consequential than the loss of research papers is the potential loss of people. Critics say the restrictions are deterring international research talent from coming to the US.
[embedded media]
A 2025 study by economists Michael Clemens and his team estimates that proposed changes to student visas and work authorisation could reduce international student enrolment by about a third and cost the US economy between US$140 billion and US$481 billion in annual GDP.
Wu said talented students, faculty members and researchers who had the freedom to choose where they worked were increasingly making decisions to avoid an environment they perceived as hostile or discriminatory.
“People who have the potential to win a Nobel Prize are people who are smart,” Wu said. “If they consider where their careers will flourish and where their lives will be happy, a place full of prejudice is not attractive.”
Surveys suggest that the political climate may also be prompting some scientists to consider leaving.
In a 2023 survey, 61 per cent of 1,304 Chinese-American faculty members said they had considered leaving the US, according to a study by Princeton sociologist Yu Xie and colleagues cited by Committee of 100.
In a March 2025 poll by the journal Nature, roughly 75 per cent of more than 1,600 US-based researchers said they were considering leaving, with Europe and Canada among their main destinations.
China’s rising strength
China’s research ecosystem, meanwhile, has followed a different trajectory over the same period, becoming both more dominant at home and more connected internationally.
According to the Institute of Scientific and Technical Information of China (ISTIC), which operates under the Ministry of Science and Technology, China accounted for 35.2 per cent of papers published in the highest-impact journals across 178 disciplines in 2024, and 39.2 per cent of papers in high-level international journals, ranking first on both measures.
As of August 2025, China also accounted for 53.2 per cent of the world’s “hot papers” – recent research ranked in the top 0.1 per cent of its field by citations – marking the first time its share had exceeded half.
Friction with Washington has not isolated Chinese science. China’s total of internationally co-authored papers reached 172,900 in 2024, up 14.4 per cent from the previous year, with research partners in 169 countries and regions. Such collaborations accounted for about a fifth of its international papers, according to ISTIC.
The US National Science Foundation is moving away from Chinese collaborators that have been flagged as restricted entities by the government. Photo: Shutterstock
China is also pulling ahead in some emerging fields. Researchers at Georgetown University’s Emerging Technology Observatory found that Chinese authors accounted for 34 per cent of research papers on chip design and fabrication published between 2018 and 2023, compared with 15 per cent for US authors – more than twice as many.
Zachary Arnold, the observatory’s lead analyst, told Nature in March 2025 that the findings did not establish that China was leading the field, but were arguably “showing us where things are headed”.
Behind that surge is sheer financial scale. China is estimated to have overtaken the US as the world’s biggest spender on research and development in 2024, with spending of US$1.03 trillion, compared with US$1.01 trillion for the US, when adjusted for purchasing power, according to the National Science Foundation’s 2026 report.
Uncertain outlook
This month’s US midterm elections may complicate the picture but are unlikely to reverse the broader trend.
Many states in the tracker are Republican strongholds, though Democrats made significant political gains.
It is unclear whether new Democratic majorities will try to repeal or amend the restrictions, especially since concerns about China remain bipartisan.
Wu predicted that US-China rivalry was locked in a clash of civilisations, putting Chinese Americans under pressure beyond geopolitics.
“The question that is asked of Chinese Americans is: which side are you on?” he said. “Nobody wanted to have to answer that.”
By Zhang Tong, Han Li

title_en: Competitive Election Committee polls critical for Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan
content_en:
The newly elected committee members have a chance to show that patriotic governance is not just a slogan but is being put into practice to make a difference.
Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse (second left), Justice David (second right) and
Electoral Affairs Commission members Daniel Shek and Bernard Man empty a ballot box at the central counting station for the Election Committee slections at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai on November 22. Photo: Sam Tsang
Hong Kong went to the polls on Sunday in another vote under the revamped governance system. While the ballot for the 1,500-member Election Committee is designed for eligible voters, the newly constituted electoral college will have a wide impact on Hong Kong’s future as it wields significant political power. The committee’s members are tasked with choosing the city’s next leader as well as a large portion of members in the legislature. title_en: Thailand agrees new durian export rules with China to protect US$5 billion trade
content_en:
New sanitation protocol – designed to raise China’s ‘confidence’ in Thai shipments – comes as durian trade between two sides surges.
A worker packs durians to be exported to China at a processing factory in Chanthaburi, Thailand. Photo: Xinhua
China and Thailand have agreed a new sanitation protocol for exports of Thai durian to raise Beijing’s “confidence” in the trade and protect billions of dollars’ worth of shipments, according to Thailand’s Ministry of Commerce.
The two governments updated plant health guidelines and procedures to clarify shipping requirements and establish a “systematic” approach to managing quarantine pests, the ministry announced on Sunday via its official website.
“This is intended to build confidence among Chinese parties, facilitate customs procedures and reduce the risk of Thai durian imports being suspended at Chinese borders,” the ministry said.
The durian protocol was “one of the most important collaborations” agreed between the two countries following Chinese Premier Li Qiang’s visit to Thailand earlier this month, according to the ministry.
China’s official Xinhua News Agency said the two nations had signed agreements on agriculture after talks between Li and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.
More than 90 per cent of Thai durians ship to China, where consumers sometimes gift the pricey, spiky and pungent fruits at formal occasions including weddings. Thailand vies with Malaysia and Vietnam as sources for the massive Chinese durian market.
Thai durian shipments to China reached 952,627 tonnes last year, valued at US$3.72 billion. In the first 10 months of 2026 alone, Thai durian exports to China reached US$5.2 billion, according to Chinese customs data.
“Any disruption to the Chinese market could seriously affect Thai durian prices, growers and exporters,” said Lim Chin Khee, an adviser to the Durian Academy, a Malaysian institution that trains growers.
“The main risk is that shipments failing China’s food safety or phytosanitary requirements could be detained, rejected or suspended,” Lim said. “A nationwide import ban is possible in serious circumstances.”
In 2025 China detected the metal cadmium in some shipments of Vietnamese durian, setting back trade in the fruit that had generated US$2.94 billion for Vietnam a year earlier.
Thai durians had also faced “quality issues” due to cadmium contamination in the past, which had affected “consumer confidence in its exports to China”, the Thai ministry said.
Fruit can absorb cadmium through the soil where it is grown. Long-term exposure to the metal can cause a range of health issues, including raising the risk of cancer.
According to the new protocol, fresh durian imported into China must be traceable through the supply chain to check for compliance.
Durian packing houses and exporters were recommended to ensure their documents and labels are consistent, the ministry said. It also called for efforts at “integrating” data from farms, packing plants and customs checkpoints.
“The new durian protocol is an opportunity for Thailand to upgrade its durian production process,” the Thai commerce ministry said.

title_en: US places Megaspeed on blacklist as Jensen Huang returns to helm of Nvidia
content_en:
The US Department of Commerce places Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm tied to Nvidia scandal, on its Entity List.
The US Department of Commerce added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist. Photo: AFP
The US Department of Commerce has added Megaspeed, the Singapore-based cloud computing firm at the centre of the ongoing Nvidia saga, to its trade blacklist, hours after the chip giant reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO following his abrupt departure 11 days prior.
In a filing released on Monday, the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security placed Megaspeed International and six other entities in Southeast Asia – widely regarded as Megaspeed’s affiliates – on its Entity List. The agency cited “the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorised end uses or end users”.
Effective immediately ahead of formal publication on Wednesday, the move blocks suppliers from shipping US-regulated technology to the blacklisted firms without first acquiring a special licence, which Washington would likely reject. Goods already in transit have a 30-day grace period.
Alongside Megaspeed International Pte Ltd – also listed under aliases including 7Road International – the blacklist targets entities across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand: Swiftdata, Apex Enterprise Solutions, Speedmatrix, MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International and Megaspeed (Thailand).
In a statement to the South China Morning Post last week, the company said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and that it had hired outside lawyers to carry out an internal investigation. It added that former executive Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday.
[embedded media]
The addition to the Entity List came on the same day Nvidia announced it reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board director. The chipmaker said it made the decision after receiving backing from US President Donald Trump and assurances from senior US officials that Huang’s return posed no national security risk.
Huang had resigned on November 12 after acknowledging extramarital affairs, triggering a sell-off across Nvidia and broader US tech stocks. Shares in the chipmaker surged more than 30 per cent on Monday following news of his return.
He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, who is suspected of acting as a Chinese spy – an allegation Beijing has firmly denied.
Washington’s trade restrictions also followed an announcement days earlier that the US Commerce and Justice departments were conducting a joint investigation into Megaspeed for potential criminal conduct.
According to the two agencies, the Commerce Department opened its inquiry in 2024 after detecting suspicious activity while monitoring for the diversion of sensitive semiconductors. The Justice Department is leading a parallel criminal investigation into possible violations of US chip export controls.
Investigators requested records from Nvidia in May 2025 regarding direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed, prompting the chipmaker to place the firm on its internal “no-sell” list the following month, the departments said.
By Ann Cao

title_en: China’s Z.ai ‘aggressively’ using looped transformer method to improve AI models
content_en:
Company is first Chinese firm to disclose using emerging technique, which offers performance gains but also raises safety concerns.
China’s Z.ai says it has used a looped transformer architecture to improve its AI models. Photo: Shutterstock
Chinese artificial intelligence company Z.ai has credited an emerging technique – one that has drawn scrutiny from AI safety researchers – with helping its newly released flagship model achieve significant performance gains over its predecessor while improving computational efficiency.
The release marks the first time a Chinese AI company has disclosed using a “looped transformer” architecture in a major model, following recent reports that US giant OpenAI adopted the same method for its newest models.
In a blog post, Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, said it “aggressively” applied the technique over the past three months, enabling its GLM-5.4 model to match the performance of AI models two to four times its size.
“This lets us raise the intelligence ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead,” the company said, noting that the technique drove improvements in mathematics, science and coding, though it withheld the detailed benchmark scores typically published alongside major model releases.
While standard transformers, the dominant architecture behind AI breakthroughs in recent years, process new data through each layer of its internal neural network once, a looped transformer passes data through the same layers multiple times.
This creates a deeper reasoning network without substantially increasing parameter count or computing costs.
That efficiency offers an edge as the global AI industry races towards massive, trillion-parameter models, which tend to deliver stronger capabilities but are vastly more expensive to train and run.
[embedded media]
Unlike domestic rivals such as Moonshot AI and DeepSeek, Z.ai has yet to release a flagship trillion-parameter model. GLM-5.4 retains the same 750-billion-parameter size as its predecessor, GLM-5.3, but performs at a level equivalent to a model in the 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameter range, according to Z.ai.
A significant scale-up also appears to be imminent. Z.ai hinted on Monday that its next model would be “significantly larger” and ready “soon”.
That aligns with a JPMorgan research note published last week, which cited an internal road map shared by Z.ai management indicating GLM-5.4 would be used to “verify training performance” ahead of a 3-trillion-parameter release by year-end aimed at “reaching the global frontier”.
Despite its efficiency gains, the looped transformer method has sparked debate over AI safety oversight and the risks of “black box” systems escaping human control.
Conventional reasoning models “think” out loud in human-readable text before generating a final answer or action, allowing researchers to monitor their logic for unwanted behaviour such as deception.
Because looped transformers reuse parts of internal neural layers, safety experts warn that a model’s decision-making process can become hidden inside those loops, making it largely opaque to human researchers.
Z.ai said GLM-5.4 spent fewer tokens on visible “thinking”, with average output length dropping up to 14 per cent on key benchmarks. “In effect, part of the reasoning shifts from explicit output tokens into the implicit depth of the loop,” the blog post said.
The safety debate gained momentum in September after US tech outlet The Information reported that OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra model would, for the first time, rely on a looped transformer to boost performance without inflating costs.
OpenAI did not confirm the report, though chief scientist Jakub Pachocki acknowledged safety concerns in subsequent social media posts, with a company representative calling the decline in model transparency “a real challenge that [it] takes seriously”.
Z.ai signalled similar caution on Monday. The company has restricted access to GLM-5.4 to its official chatbot website and coding service, saying it planned to open-source the model at an unspecified date “after completing necessary safety hardening”.

title_en: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia to applause from staff, no trademark leather jacket in sight
content_en:
Huang returns as Nvidia CEO after 11-day leadership crisis, thanking staff and saying he would “be a better CEO the second time around”.
Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia’s headquarters as CEO on Monday. Photo: Handout
When Jensen Huang walked back into Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara on Monday – without his trademark black leather jacket – the applause from cheering staff momentarily drowned out nearly two weeks of corporate turmoil.
“I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang told the crowd, joking that he would need the IT department to set him up with a computer on his first day back.
The emotional homecoming marked a stunning reversal just 11 days after Huang’s abrupt resignation plunged the artificial intelligence chip giant into a leadership crisis.

title_en: Meet the robots: China’s 6 top humanoid developers vie for market share
content_en:
What you need to know about the products of AgiBot, UBTech, Unitree and the country’s other major challengers.
Illustration: Brian Wang
Shenzhen captured the world’s attention last week as the host city of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Much of the discussion around Apec focused on the city’s transformation in just a few decades from a fishing village into what is now a hi-tech innovation hub, with one industry in particular grabbing much of the attention: humanoid robots.
As China’s hardware capital, Shenzhen has spearheaded the country’s rise to dominance in the global humanoid industry. Chinese firms will drive a near-quadrupling in global shipments of humanoids this year to 54,000 units, accounting for more than 97 per cent of international shipments in the third quarter, according to data released earlier this month by research firm Smart Analytics Global (SAG).
Chinese physical AI and humanoid robotics stocks surged on Monday – with several names, including Unitree Robotics, hitting their daily upper limits on mainland exchanges – amid growing optimism over rapid advances in the technology.
Here, South China Morning Post’s Tech and Infographics teams profile six of China’s leading humanoid robot makers.
AgiBot
Shanghai-based AgiBot topped SAG’s rankings, retaining its position as the firm with the most humanoids shipped globally at 4,900 units, equal to 30 per cent market share in the third quarter.
The high output can be explained by the company’s broad commercial strategy, with flagship robots targeting both public-facing and industrial applications. This includes the A2 robot for customer-facing work such as guided tours and the wheeled G2 robot for industrial tasks.
Founded in 2023, AgiBot has continued its “jack of all trades” strategy this year, as it pursues a Hong Kong listing. It deployed more than 300 robots in September at Chimelong Spaceship Park in the southern province of Guangdong, the world’s largest indoor theme park. That followed just a few months after it added G2 robots to the factory lines of major Chinese electronics manufacturer Longcheer, which makes Ray-Ban Meta glasses and Xiaomi smartphones.
[embedded media]
UBTech
Shenzhen-based UBTech ranked second at 4,500 units or 27 per cent of the market in the third quarter, a massive year-on-year increase of 1,603 per cent that raised the firm above Unitree Robotics.
The company, which became the first humanoid robot firm to list on the Hong Kong stock exchange in late 2023, has mainly pursued industrial applications. Its Walker S series targets logistical tasks such as moving materials and inspecting products with partners such as EV makers BYD and Nio, as well as consumer-electronics manufacturer Foxconn. It has also developed systems that connect its humanoids to autonomous logistics vehicles and manufacturing management software.
In recent months, however, the company has also made waves with its first full-size humanoid robot series, U1, designed for emotional companionship rather than industrial use. According to SAG analyst Linda Sui, UBTech’s sharp rise this year is due to accelerating industrial adoption as well as its expanding product portfolio.
[embedded media]
Unitree Robotics
Hangzhou-based Unitree came in third, with 4,400 units or a 27 per cent share, in the third quarter. The company had its initial public offering in Shanghai in August and reported revenue of 1.82 billion yuan (US$273 million) for the first nine months of 2026, up 55.7 per cent from a year earlier.
The company boasts some of the cheapest humanoids on the market, with its entry-level flagship G1 model priced at US$13,500. This has made it a popular option for research and development in both industry and academia, where it supplies the hardware for other teams to experiment on, including for development of robotics AI models.
Notable examples include Stanford University’s Autonomous Systems Lab, which uses the G1 to develop cutting-edge robot control systems. US chip giant Nvidia also announced a partnership with Unitree in June to co-create a robot reference design for research experimentation.
[embedded media]
Leju
Shenzhen-based Leju came in fourth, capturing around 3 per cent of the market with around 500 shipments in the third quarter.
The company this year continued expanding its industrial footprint through its flagship Kuavo 5 and wheeled Kuavo 5-W robots, which target automotive, home appliance manufacturing, material handling and logistics customers, according to SAG.
Its main source of revenue for its humanoids has been supplying them to data-collection centres, where the robots complete physical tasks to generate examples to train AI systems. This application accounted for 44.9 per cent of revenue for its Kuavo humanoid series last year, Leju reported in its draft prospectus in May ahead of a listing in Shenzhen.
[embedded media]
Galbot AI
Beijing-based Galbot also captured around 3 per cent of market share with around 400 shipments in the third quarter, driven by its continued focus on wheeled humanoid robots.
For members of the public, the company is increasingly associated with its “Galaxy Space” capsules: fully autonomous retail convenience stores that have reached 200 locations in around 50 Chinese cities, including three in Hong Kong.
Its flagship G1 robot, which combines a humanlike upper body with a wheeled base and adjustable torso, is marketed for retail tasks such as retrieving products from shelves and replenishing stock. Beyond retail, the company has also showcased the use of its G1 robot in pharmacy settings, including picking and packing online orders.
[embedded media]
Fourier
Founded in 2015, Shanghai-based Fourier is one of the older Chinese robot makers, though it has traditionally focused on medical rehabilitation systems and exoskeletons.
Starting in 2023, the company began expanding into humanoid robots with the launch of its GR-1 robot, while retaining its traditional healthcare focus. Its newer GR-3, launched last year, is designed for companionship and service assistance in settings including senior care.
[embedded media]

title_en: PM Wong vows to stop firms ‘exploiting’ Singapore for AI chip re-routing
content_en:
The prime minister said the city state was cooperating with the US to prevent illicit transshipments amid probe into Nvidia and Megaspeed.
Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in Canberra, Australia, on Tuesday. Photo: AFP
Singapore is working with the US to stop companies “exploiting” the country as they divert US microchips to other destinations, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Tuesday.
Wong told reporters in Australia that Singapore was not involved in the US investigation into AI chip giant Nvidia, but was conducting its own investigation into breaches by companies of Singapore law.
“We are also looking at companies that may be using Singapore and exploiting Singapore’s position to transship and divert chips through Singapore to other parts of Southeast Asia or to other countries,” Wong said.
Nvidia has been caught in a scandal since revelations of newly-reinstated boss Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman linked to Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Singapore had previously investigated Megaspeed’s Alice ‌Huang, but ‌found no basis for prosecution, Wong said.
“We took her in, we investigated her, but we eventually released ‌her because there was no basis for further prosecution,” he said.
Wong (left) shakes hands with Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra on Tuesday. Photo: AAP via Reuters
US intelligence officials reportedly suspect Megaspeed of steering Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China and the US government has said it is investigating Megaspeed over chip exports.
“The US has [a] growing interest in this area of chips coming through Singapore and being transshipped or rerouted to other countries,” Wong said.
“We are working very closely with the US administration in that regard to facilitate information sharing to work out a mechanism where America can do its own enforcement,” he added.
The Trump administration this month announced tougher export controls on AI chips, aiming to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s technology and requiring data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a licence from the US to ship advanced chips from American firms to clients in China.
In Canberra, Wong and his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese announced the two countries would deepen cooperation on AI, including exploring greater cross-border data flows.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Hacked Russian data suggests nearly 500,000 soldiers dead, reports say
content_en:
German and Russian media analysing Rosstat files point to heavy Ukraine war losses since February 2022.
Portraits of Russian soldiers at a street exhibition in St Petersburg in March. Photo: AP
Data allegedly stolen by hackers from Russia’s statistics agency Rosstat show the number of recorded Russian military dead is approaching 500,000, several Russian media outlets and German news magazine Der Spiegel reported on Monday.
The outlets said they had gained access to the data set, which the hacker groups Cyberpartisans and Silent Crow are said to have taken in an attack on the agency.
Reports say the groups are close to the Belarusian opposition or to pro-Ukrainian collectives.
Rosstat confirmed a cyberattack in early November but denied that any data had been leaked.
The outlets consider the data set they were given credible.
According to the reports, the data covers mortality in Russia. Using parameters such as the stated cause of death, place of death and occupation, the outlets said they filtered out the number of soldiers killed.
Most of the reports put the number of Russian dead at more than 490,000 from the start of Russia’s war in February 2022 until the end of September this year.
The reports point out that the actual figure is likely higher, partly because deaths are often recorded in the database with a delay.
The graves of Ukrainian soldiers in Lviv. Photo: AP
Ukraine has been defending itself against Russia’s full-scale invasion with Western support for more than four and a half years. Both sides report alleged enemy losses almost daily but rarely disclose their own casualty figures.
It is considered certain that both Russia’s leadership and that of Ukraine play down their own losses and inflate those of the enemy.
The Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) put the number of Russian dead at 400,000 to 450,000 in July. The think tank said at the time that the figure on the Ukrainian side was 125,000 to 150,000.
There are also attempts to count confirmed deaths of Ukrainian and Russian soldiers using funerals, obituaries and posts on social networks. The Russian news portal Mediazona, which said it had also analysed the hacked data set, has so far counted the names of 289,136 Russian dead.
The latest figure on the Ukrainian website UA Losses was 106,285 dead. The people behind the websites believe their tallies are incomplete.
By dpa

title_en: Malaysia’s Anwar says Beijing ‘extremely reasonable’ in South China Sea talks
content_en:
The Malaysian prime minister pushes back against criticism from Western and European leaders that conflict is looming in the disputed waters.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is interviewed by South China Morning Post Executive Editor Zuraidah Ibrahim and reporter Vincent Tan, in Shenzhen after the Apec summit on Friday. Photo: Nora Tam
China has been “extremely reasonable” in its negotiations with Malaysia over their competing claims in the South China Sea and discussions will continue as long as certain core sensitivities are respected, according to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
He said each country had “red lines” it would not compromise on: areas China considered too close to its interests, and waters Malaysia considered “undisputedly Malaysian borders”.
“OK, we don’t touch that,” he said in an interview with the South China Morning Post.
[embedded media]
This left room for flexibility elsewhere. “Then there’s give and take. They intrude a bit. We intrude a bit,” he said.
“I will have to say frankly that the Chinese have been extremely reasonable with us. We discuss. I’m not suggesting that we have concluded or agreed on all these parameters. But once you allow negotiations to take place, and we discuss and do not cross that red line, I think things are OK.”
Chinese coastguard and naval vessels have periodically patrolled waters within Malaysia’s exclusive economic zone off Borneo, overlapping with areas where Putrajaya conducts offshore oil and gas exploration.
The Malaysian prime minister pushed back against criticism from Western and European leaders who warned that Malaysia was “too close to China”, or that conflict was looming in the South China Sea. Maritime disputes, Anwar said, were a normal feature of regional diplomacy.
Malaysia had unresolved border or maritime disputes with neighbours including Singapore, Brunei, Thailand and Vietnam, yet remained “the best of neighbours” with all of them, he said, adding that the Johor–Singapore Special Economic Zone was an example of cooperation built on “trust and sanity”.
“So why take a very combative, unfriendly position vis-a-vis China?” he asked. “I say, ‘I have a problem with all my neighbours, but we are still great friends.’”
Anwar also questioned whether Beijing had shown “mischief or aggression towards anyone”, saying there were border issues and that China’s navy had been present “from a distance”.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim (left) shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping after their meeting at the Qilin Villa State Guest House on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen on Friday. Photo: dpa
Asked whether the Philippines might disagree, he acknowledged that Manila’s experience was “an exception”. Filipino officials had told him China’s approach towards the Philippines was “more aggressive, more contentious”, he said.
Even so, he said Beijing’s position remained that it was willing to negotiate as long as its red line was not crossed, and interactions he witnessed between Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr and Chinese leaders Xi Jinping and Li Qiang at Asean forums had been “very cordial”.
At the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit last week in Manila, there was a consensus that the code of conduct over the South China Sea had to be “resolved speedily, expeditiously”.
“It is interesting to note that the response by Premier Li Qiang was very positive: ‘Yes, we’ll do whatever is necessary to facilitate the process.’ You may complain in the process of negotiations, but that principle is there.”
Anwar also acknowledged that Putrajaya had expressed some concern over increased military and logistics activity at Balabac in the Philippines, near Sabah, where the US military has a presence.
However, he said Marcos had assured him that the build-up was tied to tensions with China in international waters, and unrelated to Sabah or Malaysia.
“But of course we have to monitor, even among friends,” he said.
Taipei freeze
Efforts to maintain steady ties with Beijing have also had repercussions for its relations with Taipei, which paused bilateral trade negotiations in October after Anwar said in a media interview that Taiwan was “part of China, period”.
Speaking to the SCMP, Anwar sought to downplay the freeze as a routine “two, three months” hiatus in lower-level subcommittee discussions that Putrajaya hoped to resume early next year.
He defended his controversial remark as a restatement of Malaysia’s one-China policy, which has been in place since Malaysia established diplomatic ties with the People’s Republic of China in 1974. He added that he had been pressed to take an “anti-Taiwan, anti-Pakistan” position.
“I don’t take that position. What I did was just to reinforce our position. But probably the words used can be deemed to be a bit stronger,” he said.
The pause in negotiations had not hurt broader economic ties, he said, with the latest figures showing no downward trend in investment, trade or even tourism, and major investments flowing into Malaysia remaining unaffected.
The TSMC logo is seen on screens at the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Renovation Museum in Hsinchu, Taiwan, in 2023. Photo: AFP
When asked if that included chipmaking giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, Anwar said projects were “still proceeding”, and he had been receiving updates from Malaysia’s trade and investment government bodies, including the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry and its agencies such as the Malaysian Investment Development Authority and Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation.

The Malaysian prime minister pushes back against criticism from Western and European leaders that conflict is looming in the disputed waters.

title_en: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return buoys South Korea, Japan stocks
content_en:
South Korea’s Kospi and Japan’s Nikkei surged, lifting AI-related stocks of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
In overnight trade, shares of Nvidia rose more than 30 per cent on Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. Photo: AFP
Japanese and South Korean stocks surged in early trade on Tuesday, tracking big gains on Wall Street after the shock reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
The benchmark Kospi was up 338.61 points, or 7.19 per cent, at 5,047.15 on Tuesday morning after gains triggered a five-minute “sidecar” curb on programme trading.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up 3.88 per cent at 58,623.73 points.
In overnight trade, shares of Nvidia rose more than 30 per cent on Huang’s reinstatement as CEO in a stunning reversal following his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, driving a ⁠big jump in AI-related shares.
The rebound was on track to be the Kospi’s biggest ‌since July 31. The index had fallen more than 3 per cent on Monday to its lowest level since January 13 despite policymakers pledging market-stabilisation measures to stem ‌further losses.
Analysts said there still was uncertainty over the investigations Huang would be ⁠facing, but the ⁠reinstatement helped ease deepening investor worries over the artificial intelligence boom in the short term.
“Jensen Huang’s return appears to have ‌done more than just ease CEO risk and relieve investor anxiety around the AI ecosystem,” said Han Ji-young, an analyst at ‌Kiwoom ‌Securities.
“At this point, it seems better to focus on the possibility of improving resilience in ‌stock prices while monitoring related issues, rather than the risk of an additional slump,” Han ⁠said.
[embedded media]
Chipmaker Samsung Electronics rose 8 per cent and peer SK Hynix gained 10.9 per cent, leading South Korea’s benchmark higher, ⁠on broad strength in most AI-related stocks.
Firms collaborating with Nvidia on various AI technologies also climbed, including Hyundai Motor and e-commerce firm Naver, which rose 7.7 per cent and ‌5.1 per cent, respectively, while LG Electronics ‌surged 16.7 per cent.
Online brokerage Monex said that Tokyo had been expected to start with buying, following the strong rally in the United States.

title_en: China’s historical climate records could be skewed by human bias, study finds
content_en:
Research based on data-driven evidence suggests the distortion of how extremes are interpreted stems from ‘generational amnesia’.
Researchers use China’s historical accounts of the weather – including droughts, floods and harvest conditions – to try to reconstruct and understand climate history in the region. Photo: Reuters
For centuries, scholars, officials and local chroniclers in China recorded the world around them, resulting in a collection of imperial histories, gazetteers, personal diaries and records that is seen as the most continuous in the world.
Among them are detailed accounts of the weather – including droughts, floods and harvest conditions – which researchers have used to try to reconstruct and understand the region’s climate history.
But a new study by researchers in China and Germany, based on data-driven evidence, suggests these historical records carry human bias that skewed how climate extremes were interpreted.
After comparing archival records from northern China’s Yellow River Basin over hundreds of years – from 1470 to 1900 – against natural records from tree rings, the team found that this distortion stems from a phenomenon called “generational amnesia”.
“We argue that historical archives carry a generational imprint of perceptual bias, in which the severity of climate extremes is judged against recent lived experience rather than long-term climate variability,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Communications on November 9.
“This has implications for bias-aware corrections for risk assessment, adaptation, and paleoclimate reconstruction.”
[embedded media]
Song Shuang, the study’s first author and a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, said biases in historical archives were already a “well-known phenomenon” to geographic historians.
This includes a human tendency to record abnormal events over normal ones. While this bias was known, Song said it had not been proven based on data.
“I don’t think that because of this paper, everyone needs to correct their interpretation of historical archives,” he said.
Instead, Song said it was good to be aware of the phenomenon, especially for those in the natural science field who may not be as familiar with it, which could lead to “misinterpreted phenomena”.
China’s vast historical archives have been widely used to reconstruct past climate conditions from the era before modern instruments were invented.
Among the prominent theories drawn in part from these written records is the theory that extreme weather during the Little Ice Age helped trigger the collapse of the Ming dynasty in 1644.
This theory is based on both natural climate proxies and archival data such as grain prices and famine reports.
According to the team’s paper, historical records serve as a key source of collective memory, which they define as the “storage, retrieval and forgetting of information by a society”.
“Collective memory shapes how societies respond to extreme climate events, yet long-term evidence on how the collective memory of such events becomes perceptually biased over time is lacking,” the team wrote.
The study compared archival records from the Yellow River Basin with natural proxies from tree rings. Photo: Nature
Song said this research came about when he noticed a mismatch between historical archival data and natural paleoreconstructed data, or historical climate records reconstructed using natural proxies.
After speaking with people from different fields, he learned that environmental psychology had a similar phenomenon called shifting baseline syndrome.
This describes a psychological pattern in which people judge environmental conditions – and decide what counts as “normal” – against the climate they experienced earlier in life.
It explains why different generations living side by side can experience the same weather yet hold different views of whether the climate is normal or extreme.
“I found that this theory could explain this phenomenon very well, so I started to dive into this direction,” Song said.
Collective memory inconsistencies can stem from different sources, primarily generational amnesia or collective memory illusions.
The former happens when younger generations lack knowledge of environmental conditions in the past, while the latter happens when shared narratives distort how past conditions are remembered.
To investigate the mismatch and pinpoint the source of the memory inconsistencies, the team compared human-written accounts against natural climate records.
For the historical data, the researchers drew on records from the Atlas of Extreme Droughts and Floods over the Past Millennium, a compilation of information from official histories, local gazetteers and personal diaries.
To ensure the records were mostly complete the team focused on four centuries of archives, from 1470 to 1900, spanning both the Ming and Qing dynasties.
They then compared these written accounts against natural tree-ring hydroclimate reconstructions – a method that uses annual tree-ring growth to estimate how wet and dry the growing season was, offering a baseline free from human perception.
“We show that mismatches between archival and natural records of climatic extremes in the Yellow River Basin follow a systematic pattern: archival severity is over- or underestimated when a year is only slightly wetter or drier than comparable earlier years,” the team wrote.
The natural records aligned better with the historical ones when they were re-standardised against a moving 20- to 40-year window – averaging 33 years, roughly the human lifespan at the time – instead of the entire study period.
The team’s modelling suggests that generational amnesia is sufficient to explain these inconsistencies, while collective illusion did not reproduce the same mismatch.
They acknowledged that there were limitations to their work, including inherent uncertainties in tree-ring climate reconstructions and the potential influence of changing political and institutional contexts on how disasters are recorded.
While the impact of climate amnesia today was not covered in the study, Song said he believed that we continue to compare our perceptions of the climate to a biased baseline.
“We have more and more instrumental measurements of our climate,” he said. “But I don’t think the public has a good enough awareness of its changes.”
Song said many people still made comparisons about the weather like “it’s colder than last year” and “it’s hotter than my childhood”.
He said our baseline now could be driven by things like social media, as everyone can perceive their environment and compare it with discussions online. That could be creating a collective memory-based bias, he added.
“It means an individual perceives the environment by comparing it to a collective memory or collective opinion on this matter, rather than their personal experience.”
Song said modern instrumental measurement data offered a better way to correct biased perception of the climate.
In the period studied by Song for the paper, the information flow was slow, and that could be why generational amnesia rather than a collective memory illusion was relevant.
The researchers also said their findings marked a step towards integrating collective memory into coupled human-natural models to help manage long-term disaster risks.
“As climate change accelerates, understanding how each generation responds to a new normal or baseline will become increasingly important,” they wrote.

title_en: North Korea unveils first AI chatbot, but it won’t answer ‘uncultured questions’
content_en:
The chatbot, named Fountain of Wisdom, was featured in a North Korean state television broadcast last week.
The AI chatbot (centre) is show during a report on North Korean TV on November 17. Photo: Ryongnamsan Television
North Korea appears to have unveiled its first domestic artificial intelligence chatbot, according to state television footage analysed by a US-based research programme that monitors the secretive country.
Named Fountain of Wisdom, the system was developed by Kim Il-sung University’s AI research institute alongside Phurunhanul Trading, a Pyongyang software developer, according to a report published last week by Martyn Williams, a senior fellow at the Stimson Centre, which runs the 38 North research initiative.
The chatbot was shown at an IT exhibition in Pyongyang last month and featured in a broadcast last Tuesday on the TV channel Ryongnamsan.
Featuring an interface resembling OpenAI’s ChatGPT, the tool answered science and technology queries in Korean or English and provided translations, the report said.
Chat histories visible in the broadcast included queries on game-design software and what medicine to take for a headache, Williams noted.
However, the platform came with strict ideological guardrails.
“Do not ask questions with sociopolitical content or uncultured questions,” an on-screen notice warned, according to Williams’ translation, and added that users bore responsibility for any malicious use.
While the system’s underlying architecture and hardware were not disclosed, Williams suggested it could have been built using an overseas open-weight model.
The unveiling came amid growing scrutiny over Pyongyang’s use of generative AI. North Korean hackers and IT workers already appeared to be leveraging foreign AI tools, Williams noted in his report.
In August last year, US AI developer Anthropic accused North Korean operatives of using its Claude chatbot to fabricate professional identities, pass coding assessments and carry out technical tasks after securing remote jobs at Fortune 500 technology firms.
Anthropic, which banned the accounts and shared its findings with authorities, said AI allowed operatives with limited coding or English proficiency to obtain and hold down such jobs.
By Vincent Chow, Howard Liu

title_en: Cop31 illustrated what’s wrong with climate finance
content_en:
Unless the developed world takes responsibility and the systems creating the polycrisis are re-evaluated, our problems will only get worse.
Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at the Cop31 climate talks hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall, where delegates met during the United Nations Climate Change Conference at the Antalya Expo Centre in Antalya, Turkey, on November 20. Photo: AFP
When Australia’s climate minister Chris Bowen spoke at Cop31, the United Nations climate change conference, in Antalya, Turkey, he said the world was asking whether multilateralism could rise to meet a “polycrisis” of climate change, energy security, conflict and the power demands of artificial intelligence. “Is international cooperation still a way forward? This fortnight we can answer those legitimate concerns and questions with a simple answer: Yes,” he said.
For developing countries across Asia and the wider Global South, the polycrisis is hardly new. As researcher Farwa Sial has argued, the West is only now discovering what much of the Global South has always lived with: “a continuum of so-called polycrisis”.
Multilateralism might be the only way forward. However, the question is not so much about international cooperation than the system on which the rules of cooperation rest. This system is riddled with structural power imbalances and political and economic inequalities.
Nothing illustrates this better than climate finance, and in particular what transpired in Antalya over the last two weeks. When developing countries pushed to set out how the promise to triple adaptation finance would be met, the European Union and Japan said the discussion belonged in the finance negotiations.
At talks in Bonn, Germany, in June, proposals to turn the Just Transition Mechanism into a vehicle that mobilises capital met with insistence from developed nations that finance falls outside its mandate. In an interview in October, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra called new funding demands “dead in the water”. At Cop31, a proposed US$120 billion adaptation target was dropped for a promise to discuss a pathway which did not survive.
Even the multilateral development banks, which hyped a record US$103 billion in climate finance to low- and middle-income countries in 2025, delivered around 80 per cent of their climate finance as loans and just 3.7 per cent as grants. The European Union received almost three times as much of it as sub-Saharan Africa. Meanwhile, the World Bank dropped its flagship target of directing 45 per cent of its financing to climate-related projects in June after months of pressure from the United States, its largest shareholder.

Then there is debt servicing and the fairness of how loans are structured and disbursed. title_en: Chinese drug stocks sink as US lawmakers threaten curbs on cross-border collaboration
content_en:
House committee warns ‘dangerous dependence’ on China could ‘hollow out’ US industry, calls for measures including ban on trial data.
Although just policy recommendations now, US curbs on clinical trials in China could erode the country’s biotech advantages, according to analysts. Photo: Shutterstock
Chinese healthcare stocks fell on Tuesday amid intensifying threats from Washington, where lawmakers warned about the US drug industry’s “dangerous dependence” on China and urged restrictions on cross-border collaboration.
“We cannot allow China to get ahead and control drug development, or it will use that power against us,” John Moolenaar, chairman of the US House Select Committee on China, said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that “urgent action is needed”.
The committee published a 57-page report on Tuesday, alleging that China’s “coordinated, state-sponsored industrial policy to dominate the global biotechnology sector” would “hollow out” the US industry.
To “protect and strengthen” the US biotech ecosystem, the committee made 12 policy recommendations, including restricting the US Food and Drug Administration’s acceptance of Chinese clinical trial data.
China has in recent years become an increasingly attractive destination for global drug makers to conduct early-stage clinical trials, partly because of its speed and large population of potential participants, and Moolenaar and other US lawmakers have been urging the US drug regulator to scrutinise the practice.
Five US pharmaceutical giants – AbbVie, Bristol Myers Squibb, Eli Lilly, Merck and Pfizer – would no longer start clinical trials at “sites in China run by the People’s Liberation Army”, the committee said on Tuesday, adding that all but AbbVie would also end trials in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region.
Although broader curbs on clinical trials in China had not yet moved beyond policy recommendations, potential US restrictions could erode the country’s biotech advantage, analysts said previously.
China’s biopharmaceutical industry showed little reaction to the committee’s latest findings, just as it did last week following a separate report by a US congressional advisory body warning against American reliance on Chinese pharmaceutical ingredients.
Chinese healthcare stocks, however, fell on Tuesday after gaining on Monday. The Hang Seng Biotech Index dropped more than 1.5 per cent on Tuesday after a 2.62 per cent gain on Monday, and major Chinese drug makers Sino Biopharmaceutical and 3SBio declined 2.61 per cent and 3.75 per cent, respectively, in Hong Kong.
Wuxi AppTec and Wuxi Biologics, two of China’s biggest contract biopharmaceutical service providers, lost 1.69 per cent and 1.31 per cent, respectively, wiping out the bulk of their gains on Monday.
Geopolitical risks remained a focal point for many investors watching China’s healthcare sector, JPMorgan’s head of China healthcare research Yang Huang said last week.
The US Treasury Department proposed new rules last month under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (Coins) Act, which aimed to restrict US biotech equity investments and joint ventures involving countries including China.
The Coins Act rules, if approved, would pose major disruptions to cross-border deals. The department is soliciting feedback on the draft until December 18.
By Xinmei Shen

title_en: ‘Not true’: Anwar denies Malaysian government leaked Najib pardon minutes
content_en:
The prime minister has called for an investigation into how the document came to be circulated prematurely.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has denied that the pardon minutes were leaked by the legal affairs division of the Prime Minister’s Department or the Attorney General’s Chambers. Photo: AFP
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Tuesday denied that the Malaysian government circulated Pardons Board minutes related to disgraced former leader Najib Razak’s house arrest, calling for an investigation into the controversy swirling around his administration.
Anwar said certain sections of the document were declassified by the attorney general for submission to court regarding the case.
“Don’t make accusations that the government circulated it. It did not. That is not true,” he told parliament.
Anwar’s clarification came after lawmaker Ahmad Fadhli Shaari asked why the minutes were revealed through the media rather than through official channels.
He also rejected accusations that the notes of the September 18 meeting, chaired by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, were leaked by the legal affairs division of the Prime Minister’s Department or the Attorney General’s Chambers.
Anwar said the document became public following its presentation in court, but how the media obtained it early should be investigated, Free Malaysia Today reported.
“The home ministry should investigate how it came to be circulated prematurely,” he said.
According to the minutes, Attorney General Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar and Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh opposed allowing Najib to serve the rest of his prison sentence at home until his scheduled release in August 2028.
Malaysian’s former prime minister Najib Razak waves to the media as prison officers escort him at the Kuala Lumpur High Court complex on November 10. Photo: AP
However, the king granted Najib’s request, provided he paid a 50 million ringgit (US$12.1 million) fine. The former prime minister’s party eventually settled the penalty, and he left prison for his Kuala Lumpur residence earlier this month.
Najib has been in jail since 2022 after being found guilty of corruption and money laundering in a case linked to the scandal-hit state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad.
Anwar also maintained that the government was transparent in handling the issue and that the resulting furore was exaggerated.
“Besides, for those of us who talk about freedom and transparency, what is the problem?”
When asked why the minutes regarding his 2018 royal pardon had not been divulged, Anwar said the court sought only the clemency decision, not the notes.
“Had the minutes been requested, it would have been up to the attorney general and the court to decide whether they could be declassified in that case,” he said.
Then king Sultan Muhammad V granted a full royal pardon to Anwar, who was sentenced to a five-year jail term for charges of sodomy the politician said were trumped up by Najib.
The political storm over Najib’s pardon is expected to roar back in the coming months when a court hears the Malaysian Bar’s judicial review application challenging his house arrest order.
The Attorney General’s Chambers on Tuesday said it would oppose the petition during a hearing scheduled for next March, adding that decisions made by the king under the federal constitution were non-justiciable.
By SCMP’s Asia desk

title_en: ‘People are going to die’: Thailand’s toxic rivers, ‘zombie’ fish sow dread
content_en:
Arsenic from unregulated Myanmar mines is poisoning waterways, fuelled by a rare earth trade Thais also profit from.
Activists shouts slogans during a protest on Sunday in Chiang Rai against rare earth mining in Myanmar, which has been linked to river contamination in northern Thailand. Photo: Reuters
Every November, or thereabouts, Thais float candlelit baskets down rivers to carry away the year’s bad luck.
Prajak Kruasree, a 68-year-old village elder in Mae Sai, Chiang Rai province, used to watch the Sai River come alive with those small, flickering lights.
But this year, he says his community cannot pay its respects to the water as part of the annual Loy Krathong festival – because the water has been poisoned.
“There is no tap water,” Prajak told This Week in Asia. “The province announced a ban on using the water. Farmers are hit hard. The rice mills have stopped buying.”
Happier times: people in northern Thailand’s Chiang Mai province release candlelit boats in a pond to celebrate Loy Krathong festival in 2020. Photo: AFP
A toxic river crisis has engulfed northern Thailand, contaminating drinking water, threatening crops and sparking alarm over deformed fish, as villagers have been told to keep away from rivers that have sustained them for generations.
“They announced that every kind of vegetable is contaminated,” Prajak said. “Now the whole province is being branded together as a contaminated province: Chiang Rai rice, Mae Sai rice, all of it is branded as poisoned goods.”
Subsequent tests on dozens of rice samples found that none exceeded safety limits – and by Sunday, local rice mills had reportedly resumed purchases.
For farmers like Prajak, however, the stigma of contamination has already done the damage.
Thai authorities, supported by scientific findings, say unsafe levels of arsenic and other heavy metals have been found in the Sai, Kok and Ruak rivers.
All three rise in Myanmar’s Shan state, where dozens of mines scouring the earth for gold and rare earths – the elements that make EV batteries, wind turbines and other new technologies possible – are thought to operate.
A photo circulating on social media shows a deformed fish recently caught in northern Thailand. Photo: Facebook
Orange rivers, ‘zombie’ fish
The crisis first surfaced last year, when the Kok River turned orange.
As villagers complained about the pollution, images began to circulate online showing pools filled with chemicals used to “leach” rare earths from the ground in Myanmar – a process that involves pumping acid-laced water into mountainsides to separate the ores.
More mines have since been uncovered through the use of satellite imagery analysis and open-source intelligence, as rising demand drives miners deeper into the mountains, without oversight, pollution controls or restraint.
And the pollution just keeps on coming, despite the desperate pleas of villagers whose livelihoods and safety are at stake.
An Thai activist holds a floating basket used for the Loy Krathong festival bearing the message “Stop mining” beside the Sai River during a protest on Sunday against rare earth mining in Myanmar. Photo: Reuters
Earlier this month, pictures of so-called zombie fish covered in welts and deformities – a result, activists suspect, of the toxins now flowing through their habitat – went viral. The affected species is a staple catch for Mekong River communities.
The images horrified Thais downstream, including in Bangkok, who began questioning what it was they were eating and where exactly it had come from.
It also added urgency to the government’s response. Officials, acting through national security mechanisms, have announced plans to ban the export and transit of chemicals used in rare earth mining, designate part of the Kok River a pollution-control zone from next month and expand water testing in affected communities.
“We need a precise fingerprint of this matter,” Thailand’s science minister Yodchanan Wongsawat, who was himself born in Chiang Mai, said on Sunday.
Thai science minister Yodchanan Wongsawat (second from right) receives a letter from activists during a protest on Sunday against rare earth mining in Myanmar. Photo: Reuters
Yodchanan, who is also a deputy prime minister, called for careful documentation of what was happening, where the pollution came from and who was affected. “Simply making accusations is not enough – we must have scientific evidence.”
His Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation confirmed in a social media post on Monday that the arsenic contaminating northern Thailand’s Kok and Sai rivers was not natural background mineral deposits but new pollution flowing across the border from upstream.
Citing environmental forensics undertaken by Thailand Science Research and Innovation – a government agency that has used chemical fingerprinting, satellite imagery and sediment tests to map the crisis – it said 60 to 75 per cent of the arsenic in the Kok River was linked to rare earth mines, with about 26 per cent from gold mines.
In the Sai River, nearly two-thirds of the excess toxins present were traced to gold mines and 29 per cent to rare earth mines, it added.
‘People are going to die’
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul says his government has raised the issue with both Myanmar, where the mines are located, and with China, the end customer for much of the rare earths and other ores mined there.
Trilateral meetings are also expected to be held this week, starting on Tuesday.
Yet Thais have long profited from the trade too. At least some of the ore mined in Shan state is exported through Thailand, with Thai companies, brokers and logistics networks acting as middlemen – as Myanmar and Chinese operators also line their pockets.
[embedded media]
Phattarapong Leelaphat, an opposition MP from the populist People’s Party, has accused the Thai government of dragging its feet and failing to hold Myanmar and China to account for the pollution linked to upstream mining.
“We are letting our country become a transit route … letting businesses with 100 per cent Chinese shareholders import ore from Myanmar and export it onwards, while we still lack the rules to control it,” he told parliament on November 19, in a stinging rebuke of the government.
“As for the country behind the source … Thailand doesn’t dare talk to them either.”
For Prajak’s community and others like it that rely on the country’s rivers for their livelihoods, it is a fight for survival.
Businesses were using Thailand’s rivers as “a dumping ground for their mud and their toxic waste”, he said.
“If they stop importing and exporting the raw materials or precursors, that’s the end of it. The mines stop and the mud and poison stop coming.”
If not, Prajak warned: “People are going to die.”

Thai science minister Yodchanan Wongsawat (second from right) receives a letter from activists during a protest on Sunday against rare earth mining in Myanmar. Photo: Reuters
Yodchanan, who is also a deputy prime minister, called for careful documentation of what was happening, where the pollution came from and who was affected. “Simply making accusations is not enough – we must have scientific evidence.”
His Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation confirmed in a social media post on Monday that the arsenic contaminating northern Thailand’s Kok and Sai rivers was not natural background mineral deposits but new pollution flowing across the border from upstream.
Citing environmental forensics undertaken by Thailand Science Research and Innovation – a government agency that has used chemical fingerprinting, satellite imagery and sediment tests to map the crisis – it said 60 to 75 per cent of the arsenic in the Kok River was linked to rare earth mines, with about 26 per cent from gold mines.
In the Sai River, nearly two-thirds of the excess toxins present were traced to gold mines and 29 per cent to rare earth mines, it added.
‘People are going to die’
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul says his government has raised the issue with both Myanmar, where the mines are located, and with China, the end customer for much of the rare earths and other ores mined there.
Trilateral meetings are also expected to be held this week, starting on Tuesday.
Yet Thais have long profited from the trade too. At least some of the ore mined in Shan state is exported through Thailand, with Thai companies, brokers and logistics networks acting as middlemen – as Myanmar and Chinese operators also line their pockets.
[embedded media]
Phattarapong Leelaphat, an opposition MP from the populist People’s Party, has accused the Thai government of dragging its feet and failing to hold Myanmar and China to account for the pollution linked to upstream mining.
“We are letting our country become a transit route … letting businesses with 100 per cent Chinese shareholders import ore from Myanmar and export it onwards, while we still lack the rules to control it,” he told parliament on November 19, in a stinging rebuke of the government.
“As for the country behind the source … Thailand doesn’t dare talk to them either.”
For Prajak’s community and others like it that rely on the country’s rivers for their livelihoods, it is a fight for survival.
Businesses were using Thailand’s rivers as “a dumping ground for their mud and their toxic waste”, he said.
“If they stop importing and exporting the raw materials or precursors, that’s the end of it. The mines stop and the mud and poison stop coming.”
If not, Prajak warned: “People are going to die.”

title_en: Kim Ju-ae’s luxury ski gear; Elon Musk developing Philippine islands: 7 Asia highlights
content_en:
From Najib Razak’s house arrest to Takaichi’s attendance at the Apec summit, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
Kim Ju-ae, daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, skis at a tourist zone under development in Samjiyon, North Korea, on Sunday. Photo: KCNA via AP
We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing.
1. Kim Jong-un’s daughter wears European ski gear worth over a year’s pay
Kim Ju-ae, the daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has drawn attention after official photos of her hitting the slopes at a ski resort under development sparked speculation over the cost of her outfit.
2. Elon Musk quietly developing ‘1 or 2’ Philippine islands, Manila envoy says
Tesla CEO Elon Musk attends the “A New Golden Age” summit at the US Institute of Peace in Washington, in October. Photo: Reuters
Elon Musk may be developing one or two islands in the Philippines, according to the country’s ambassador to the United States, who said the world’s richest man was “very interested” in the Southeast Asian nation.
3. Japan’s PM faces icy Apec summit as support for China policy slides
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi arrived at the Apec summit in Shenzhen with public backing for her China policy at its lowest since she took office 13 months ago.
4. Former Malaysian minister calls on Indonesia to pay US$3 billion for haze losses
Visitors look out at the hazy Kuala Lumpur skyline on October 16. Photo: AP
Malaysia’s former finance minister Lim Guan Eng called on Indonesia to compensate the country for economic and welfare losses – estimated at 13 billion ringgit (US$3 billion) – arising from this year’s haze crisis, or agree to form a permanent transboundary task force to tackle future fires.
5. US envoy slams New Zealand mayor over ‘unfathomable’ democracy, Beijing remarks
The US ambassador to New Zealand sharply criticised Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown after the mayor said democracy had “had its day” and praised China’s governance and economic model.
6. Baton rogue: Trump asks Philippines for MacArthur-style honour, gets polite no
United States President Donald Trump (left) and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr toast during a lunch at the Malacanang Palace in Manila on Wednesday. Photo: Reuters
The Philippine military has clarified that a gold baton awarded to the late American general Douglas MacArthur is no longer part of its honours system, dampening a demand for a similar accolade from US President Donald Trump.
7. Malaysia’s Pardons Board minutes expose legal rift over Najib’s house arrest
Malaysia’s attorney general objected to former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest, saying it had no legal basis – but the king approved the arrangement, newly disclosed Pardons Board minutes showed, fuelling a debate over the limits of royal clemency powers.
By SCMP

title_en: Late pope’s diary recounts seeing the devil, gates of hell
content_en:
A new book drawn from former pontiff’s journal reveals spiritual struggles, regrets and reflections on mortality.
Pope Francis in 2024. Francis, who ​led the Church for 12 years until his death in April 2025, experienced visions of the devil and hell. Photo: AFP
The late Pope Francis saw the devil three times and once saw the “gates of hell”, he revealed in his personal diary, excerpts of which were published Tuesday in a new book.
The Private Diary of Pope Francis, by Argentine Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernandez, includes passages taken from a journal the former Jorge Bergoglio kept between 1992 and 2024, a document that reveals his worries, regrets and self-critiques – as well as his enormous humanity and faith.
Fernandez, head of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, said he was asked by Francis to help make known to the world the musings inside the black plastic journal.
Upon Francis’ death last year, Fernandez expressed concern to his successor, Leo XIV, that the book would be “left forgotten in some storage”. He was allowed to publish passages, noting that “the spiritual concerns present in his (Francis’) heart are very clear and can do us good”.
In one of the most intriguing revelations, Francis writes that while archbishop of Buenos Aires, he saw the devil three different times including “from the car while I was going home, and in the choir during the mass”, and once in Rome following a visit to Chile.
“I discovered that the demon was prowling brazenly, hovering cunningly,” wrote Francis in his journal on January 24, 2021, according to an advance copy of the French language version of the book published by Albin Michel and viewed by Agence France-Presse.
Copies of ‘The Private Diary of Pope Francis’. Photo: Reuters
Francis wrote that he recalled three episodes “where I’m sure he actually appeared physically”.
“About 15 years ago. I saw him from the car window. I won’t forget his threatening and, at the same time, alluring eyes,” he wrote.
During the second episode inside a Carmelite chapel, Francis wrote: “He looked at me with flaming eyes.
“I won’t forget that look, more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire.”
The third episode occurred during a meeting in Rome, following a visit to Chile.
“I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything … I can’t forget the powerful rasp of his voice,” he wrote, adding that “the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters”.
Pope Francis in a car before boarding the papal plane in 2024. Photo: Reuters
Francis also revealed, on June 7, 2018, that on the night before, while getting ready to go to sleep, he “saw the gates of hell”.
“Pagan seduction in all its force. I watched a little, and it terrified me,” he said, adding that he “took the rosary as a weapon”.
“It’s dangerous to get close to the gates of hell, because flames can spring out and burn,” he wrote.
Throughout the diary, Francis does not hesitate to criticise himself, for his occasional “feelings of disdain, envy, pride” or for having ignored a drunk man in the street who addressed him “because I wanted to walk in peace and quiet”.
“The arrogant, self-sufficient, cynical Jorge who lies to himself,” is how the former pope described himself on December 30, 2022.
On January 15, 2017, he confessed that “for the past three or four days, I’ve been really angry and upset”.
While charismatic, Pope Francis also had a strong personality and was sometimes criticised within the Curia, the Catholic Church’s governing body, for being authoritarian.
Mercy is a recurrent theme in the journal.
“In hindsight, I realised all the harm I’ve caused in my life. How much of the Lord’s mercy I need!” he wrote on January 5, 1997.
Pope Francis appeared to worry that his days on Earth would be short-lived, fretting over his ageing and the need to “deal with it”.
In 1996, at age 60 – nearly three decades before his death – he wrote: “I want to do good with the little time I have left, hoping to be kind.
“How much time wasted, how much harm done!”
In 2001, he wrote that “the age of 65 makes me think of the end. I’m already counting down”.
The worries continued even after becoming pope in 2013, with Francis writing on April 9, 2016 that “the devil’s attacks, in different forms, have increased … Is this a sign that time is running out and he doesn’t want to lose?”
The journal contains 86 pages written before his election as pope in 2013, and another 55 afterwards.
One of the briefest – and most moving – passages in Francis’ diary comes on July 21, 2013: “On March 13, they elected me pope”.
Francis died on April 21, 2025.
By Agence France-Presse
