title_en: Malaysia’s Anwar rejects claims he is ‘too pro-Chinese’
content_en:
After a third state poll defeat, the prime minister tells SCMP he can win back Malay voters and dismisses talk of a snap general election.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim speaks to the South China Morning Post in Shenzhen on Friday. Photo: Nora Tam
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has pushed back against claims that he is “too pro-Chinese” and said he was confident of winning back Malay voters after his party failed to win a single seat in the Melaka state election, the third state defeat for his coalition this year.
“To me, Malays and Chinese are my people,” Anwar said in an interview with the South China Morning Post, conceding that while his government’s policies had benefited the country, the effects might not have been evenly felt.
“The big ‘but’ is that he [Anwar] is too pro-Chinese,” he said. “Then you have to go down and explain. ‘Is it true? No’ … I’m a Malay. I’m a Muslim. I have Islamic programmes. And Malay bumiputra programmes.”
“But I will not sit as prime minister and entertain this racism and religious demagoguery. I will not, so we will have to navigate … And I am pretty optimistic,” he added.
I will not sit as prime minister and entertain this racism and religious demagogueryMalaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim
Asked whether Malay support would return, Anwar said he was confident voters would back him at the parliamentary level.
On his Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition’s poor performance in recent state elections and his ability to stay in office, he said the two were distinct and he was “still in good shape” to serve out a full term.
His People’s Justice Party (PKR) “didn’t get one seat in the last election”, he conceded, referring to the Melaka poll. “We didn’t get one seat in this election. But now Anwar is prime minister because of parliamentary support, not state support.”
PH, the coalition Anwar leads, won four of Melaka’s 28 elected seats in the election on November 14, down from five during the last state election in 2021. PH member the Democratic Action Party (DAP) held all four of the seats it won in 2021. Anwar’s PKR and coalition partner Amanah lost every seat they contested.
Pakatan Harapan supporters attend an event last month announcing the coalition’s candidates for the Melaka state election. Photo: Facebook/ChanFoongHin
Anwar played down the idea that the latest results in Melaka, or earlier this year in Johor, were markedly different from previous contests in 2021 and 2022, respectively.
“What difference, very little difference, I think the analytics must go much deeper,” he said.
PH’s rivals, the Umno-led Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition and the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party, together won roughly the same number of votes in Melaka as they did in the 2022 general election, when they contested separately, said Ibrahim Suffian, co-founder and programmes director of the Merdeka Centre for Opinion Research in Malaysia.
Asked whether PH had lost ground among Malay voters, Ibrahim said: “Support largely stayed the same, but aggregate votes reduced a little due to lower turnout.”
About 3 per cent of votes also went to Bersama, he added, referring to the political party taken over earlier this year by Anwar’s former political deputy Rafizi Ramli.
‘It’s not Umno’
Malaysia’s prime minister acknowledged the pressure on the federal Madani government, as his unity administration is known, citing subsidies and financial assistance as measures taken to help voters. “I’m not oblivious to the stark realities,” he said. “There are pressures.”
Anwar spoke to the South China Morning Post in Shenzhen, where he attended last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting and held bilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Meanwhile, he also pushed back against suggestions that federal coalition party the United Malays National Organisation was pressing for a snap general election.
He declined to attribute the calls for a snap poll to “some minions within Umno”, asking “Has Umno done that? … It’s not Umno.”
Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi (centre) celebrates Barisan Nasional’s victory in Melaka’s state election on November 14. He appeared to call for a snap general election earlier this month. Photo: Iman Muttaqin Yusof
On November 10, Umno’s president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi – who is also deputy prime minister and BN chairman – had said dissolving parliament would be preferable to a cabinet reshuffle, following DAP secretary general Anthony Loke’s announcement that he was resigning as transport minister.
However, Zahid later said BN remained committed to supporting Anwar at the federal level, despite their rivalry in state elections.
Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre think tank in Kuala Lumpur, called Zahid’s comment a “spur of the moment exuberant call” by the deputy prime minister, as Umno rode from one “spectacular” state victory to the next.
“A serious push would see Umno indeed withdrawing support, as it did under Zahid in 2021,” Oh said.
In August 2021, Muhyiddin Yassin resigned as Malaysia’s prime minister after several Umno MPs, including Zahid, withdrew their backing and Muhyiddin lost his parliamentary majority. This paved the way for his deputy, Umno’s Ismail Sabri Yaakob, to succeed him without a general election.
Asked whether he would still be prime minister in 2028, when the next general election is due, Anwar smiled and replied: “Ah, that you ask Malaysians.”
By Vincent Tan

title_en: China corruption watchdog investigates senior science ministry official Liu Min
content_en:
The former director of major technology projects faces a joint investigation by the central CCDI team and Hubei provincial authorities.
Liu Min, a senior Chinese science ministry official, is being investigated by anti-corruption authorities. Photo: Handout
Liu Min, a senior official at the Ministry of Science and Technology, is under investigation, according to China’s top anti-corruption watchdog, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI).
Liu is “suspected of serious violations of party discipline and national laws” – a euphemism for corruption – and is subject to disciplinary review by the CCDI team at the ministry.
She was also being investigated by the supervisory commission in Yichang, Hubei province, in central China, the CCDI said in a statement on Monday.
Liu, who has worked at the science ministry for more than a decade, was named deputy director of its Department of Innovation and Development in 2014.
A year later she became director of the ministry’s Intellectual Property Affairs Centre and in 2020 was appointed director of the Department of Major Science and Technology Projects.
[embedded media]
Public records show that this department was in charge of developing proposals and planning major national projects, as well as monitoring and overseeing project implementation, issuing supporting policies and organising evaluations.
In 2023, after institutional reform, the ministry removed the department and integrated its core functions into other divisions.
The reform was part of a plan to assert more Communist Party control over crucial domains such as science and technology, finance and grass-roots governance, at a time of fierce technological competition with the United States.
The authorities were concerned with the need to achieve breakthroughs and move the country faster towards self-reliance while striving against the US for leading position in the technology race.

title_en: China races to develop home-grown photoresists as Japanese export curbs squeeze chipmakers
content_en:
The global market is currently dominated by Japanese firms, which accounted for more than 53 per cent of worldwide photoresist output in 2025.
An interior view of a wafer fabrication line at a company in the Western Science City in southwest China’s Chongqing municipality, August 24, 2023. Photo: Xinhua
Facing tightening scrutiny by Japanese exporters, China – the world’s largest consumer of photoresist – is accelerating the development of domestic alternatives for the critical silicon-wafer manufacturing material to bolster supply chain security and self-reliance.
The country’s photoresist sector is set for rapid expansion, with Frost & Sullivan forecasting a 13.4 per cent compound annual growth rate over the next five years. The mainland Chinese market, which generated 7 billion yuan (US$1.05 billion) in revenue in 2025, is projected to hit 13.1 billion yuan by 2030.
Growth will mainly be driven by high-end applications, including ArF and KrF photoresist, as domestic suppliers push beyond mature-node offerings, the consultancy noted.
Currently, the global market is dominated by Japanese firms. Estimates from industrial equipment manufacturer Seishin Trading placed Japan’s share of worldwide photoresist production between 50 and 80 per cent in December 2025, with JSR and Tokyo Ohka Kogyo named among the country’s major suppliers.
“The photoresist market is set for further expansion, fuelled by the artificial intelligence boom,” said Li Yang, analyst at Shanghai-based Sinolink Securities. “China remains heavily dependent on imports of high-end photoresist.”
“With Japan tightening supply and uncertainties ahead, home-grown alternatives are imperative.”
A year ago, Japan revised its Export Trade Control Order, placing high-end photoresists, including ArF and EUV grades, under case-by-case export licensing. Review windows were extended from 30 days to 90 days, with roughly 110 Chinese semiconductor firms subject to tighter scrutiny, according to Li.
Photoresist is a light-sensitive material used to transfer circuit patterns onto silicon wafers during lithography and is considered a critical input for chipmaking. It is categorised by exposure wavelength. Among its variants, the KrF, ArF and EUV grades represent the most advanced types and now constitute major supply chokepoints for China.
China needs to secure self-reliance. The photoresist industry has no alternative but to build local capacityZhou Zheng, Aijian Securities
Data from the China Electronic Materials Industry Association showed that domestic penetration for KrF was about 3 per cent in 2025, while ArF penetration was below 1 per cent.
“Low penetration carries risks, but it also points to growth potential and room for upside,” said Zhou Zheng, an analyst at Shanghai-based Aijian Securities. “China needs to secure self-reliance. The photoresist industry has no alternative but to build local capacity.”
The mainland capital market has taken note. Even amid broad A-share sell-offs, stocks in the photoresist sector had climbed more than 4.4 per cent this month by noon on Tuesday.
“Home-grown substitution has long been a market catalyst for China’s tech shares,” Zhou added.
Li Yang from Sinolink Securities said Chinese firms were conducting research and development (R&D) while reverse-engineering the original formulation from finished photoresist products. On the downstream side, customer validation typically took two to three years.
Chinese authorities are stepping up support for the photoresist sector with local governments channelling fiscal resources into the industry.
The southern tech hub of Shenzhen offers backing for photoresist industrial projects, with a cap of 10 million yuan. Also, Xiamen in southeast China’s Fujian province provides grants of up to 20 per cent of R&D, with an annual ceiling of 5 million yuan per company.
Under the 15th five-year plan for the development of the electronic information manufacturing industry released in September, China will launch a special initiative for the high-end upgrading of electronic components and electronic materials to “shore up weakness in key semiconductor materials”. Photoresist falls into this category of electronic materials.

title_en: Presidential suite? Trump’s stay turns Shenzhen hotel into viral sensation
content_en:
Chinese visitors flock to the hotel where US president stayed during Apec summit; many ask why he did not pick a more expensive venue.
People pose for pictures from an overpass near The Langham hotel ahead of the Apec meetings in Shenzhen last week. Photo: Reuters
A hotel in central Shenzhen has become the city’s latest tourist hotspot in recent days, after US President Donald Trump made the venue his base for the Apec summit.
Visitors have flocked to The Langham in the days since the summit ended last week, with many curious to discover why the US leader had chosen a hotel from a non-American chain that is cheaper than other five-star resorts nearby.
Photos posted on the social platform RedNote showed crowds of people thronging The Langham’s facilities over the weekend. Some users even claimed to have booked stays in the hotel’s presidential suites.
Many praised Trump’s team for its frugality, as nightly rates at The Langham – opened in 2012 – were much lower than newer properties nearby, including outlets run by US chains Marriott, Hilton and Hyatt.
The Langham charges only about 1,000 yuan (US$150) per night for a standard room in late November, whereas the Park Hyatt in Shenzhen is priced at 2,800 yuan, according to major booking platforms.
The presidential suite at The Langham, where Trump may have stayed, costs 30,000 yuan per night, compared with 100,000 yuan at the Park Hyatt.
Still, The Langham likely ticked all the right boxes for Trump, according to a hospitality consultant.
“In planning VIP and presidential trips, security, logistical support and room numbers take precedence over luxury,” said Xi Shao, a market analyst with Beijing-based hotel and accommodation consultancy Lujie Travel.
“In publicly available procurement records for US presidential trips, there are several considerations: a hotel’s competence in hosting large VIP delegations, proximity to event venues and infrastructure supporting top-level security deployment,” he added in an article published on Saturday.
“Once security requirements are met, another top goal is how to accommodate a very large delegation – where the president himself stays is just part of the overall practical considerations,” Xi said in a separate reply to the South China Morning Post, adding that Trump’s entourage needed more than 200 rooms for the Shenzhen stay.
“Most newer hotels in Shenzhen do not have enough rooms, but The Langham does, with a meaningful buffer of rooms to suit diversified needs, including meetings and other functions,” he added.
Conrad Shenzhen is also attracting crowds of visitors, after the hotel hosted Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Apec summit. Photo: Handout
The Langham Shenzhen has 352 rooms, according to its website. It is managed by Langham Hotels International, a brand with British heritage that is headquartered in Hong Kong. The hotel in Shenzhen was built by and belongs to a private local conglomerate, Shenzhen Donghai Group.
During his stay at the hotel, Trump met Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, according to White House press releases.
Another hotel in Shenzhen, the Conrad – part of a luxury chain owned by Hilton – is also attracting visitors after Russian President Vladimir Putin stayed there during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meetings.
Across the city, crowds have flocked to the Shenzhen International Communication Centre, the main venue for the leaders’ summit and welcome banquet.
The centre’s hotel, managed by British hotel chain InterContinental, aims to capitalise on the Apec frenzy as it prepares to open bookings to the public.
“We believe full bookings, a full house, from now to the end of the year,” local media quoted the hotel’s management as saying. “Many are curious to check out the Apec venue and menu.”
Shenzhen had hoped for just such a post-Apec boom for local businesses, as the city looks to stay on the radar of global media and tourists.
As the city clears away the road barricades and pares back security measures following the summit, official media have called for fresh strategies to boost tourism.
“Apec allowed the world to see Shenzhen and Guangdong. The next question is whether the world will still want to return and stay, now that the event has ended,” read a Friday editorial in the Yangcheng Evening News, an official publication in southern China’s Guangdong province, where Shenzhen is located.
“We need to sustain the Apec attention and traffic for as long as possible. Capitalising on people’s curiosity and opening and promoting some summit facilities and hotels to visitors can be part of the package.”
By Frank Chen
